The lamp on the windowsill flickered once, as if remembering how to breathe, then settled into a dimness too quiet to call shadow.  
Outside, a single leaf skidded across the pavement—not falling, not dancing, just drifting, as though the air had forgotten its name.  
No one passed by. No breath stirred the curtain. The house held its silence like a secret too heavy to speak, too tired to keep.

The bulb flickered once, as if forgetting how to stay lit, its glow thin as breath on glass.  
A shadow slipped across the floor—not quite movement, not quite absence—leaving only the ghost of a pulse in the dust.  
No one came, no one called; the air held its silence like a secret too heavy to speak.

The lamp on the windowsill flickered once, as if remembering it had once been brighter.  
Outside, a cat stepped over a fallen leaf—no sound, no pause—and vanished into the hush between breaths.  
No one came to close the door, and the air, thin with absence, held the weight of something never quite said.

The lamp on the windowsill flickered once, as if forgetting how to stay lit.  
Outside, a leaf trembled in a breath of air that didn’t quite count as wind.  
No one came to the door, and the silence didn’t so much settle as dissolve—quietly, uselessly, like a name no one remembered to call.

The light hung thin, barely enough to blush the dust motes into visibility, as if the sun had forgotten to turn up the dial.  
A breath of motion stirred the curtain—not a wind, not a sigh, just the faintest tremor in the air, like a held thought refusing to leave.  
No one was there, but the chair remembered sitting.
